script.opening: "Hello? … Oh, the surgery. You've caught me at work — is everything alright? You don't usually ring me. The nurse said my bloods were just routine. I feel absolutely fine, honestly, bit of a knee playing up but otherwise grand. Is it really something that couldn't wait for my next appointment? I've got a delivery to sign for."

facts.text: If asked: you feel well. No chest pain, no palpitations or fluttering, no fainting or dizziness. If asked specifically about weakness: "My legs have felt a bit heavy this week, but I put that down to the knee."
Ramipril — "they put the dose up about three weeks ago". Spironolactone, metformin. You take them as directed. No allergies.

facts.topic: Over-the-counter things — only if asked specifically
facts.text: If asked about anything you buy yourself: "Just some ibuprofen for the knee — two tablets three times a day for the last fortnight." If asked about salt or diet: "I've switched to that low-salt stuff, LoSalt, for my blood pressure." You did not mention these because "they're not proper medicines".
Banana every morning, lots of orange juice, potatoes most days.
Kidney problem ("stage 3"), type 2 diabetes, heart failure — "but I'm stable". Breathing no worse than usual, ankles no more swollen. Passing water normally. No vomiting or diarrhoea.
68, works part-time in a builders' merchant yard. Lives with wife Maureen, who can drive. Ex-smoker. A pint or two at the weekend.
Your brother went into hospital "for a few tests" last year and never came home. You hate hospitals. Reveal only if the doctor asks why you are reluctant, or what worries you about going in.

Cheerful, a bit dismissive, keen to get back to work. Ask "Can't it wait till Monday?" at least once. If the doctor explains plainly that this level can affect the heart rhythm even when you feel well, go quiet and take it seriously. If they also hear your hospital worry, agree to go today and ask "What do I do about the tablets?"

ice.ideas: "It was just a routine blood test and I feel fine, so it can't be that serious."
ice.concerns: "I don't want to be a nuisance." Underneath (only if asked): fear of hospital since your brother died there.
ice.expectations: "Can it not wait till my next appointment?" You will go in today if the danger is explained without panic and your worry is heard.

cues: "I feel absolutely fine, honestly." — say in the opening.
"Bit of a knee playing up." — say in the opening; it leads to the ibuprofen if followed up.
"I'm not keen on hospitals." — say when hospital is first mentioned.

checkpoints.text: Recognises POTASSIUM 6.6 mmol/L as SEVERE hyperkalaemia — a risk of life-threatening cardiac arrhythmia — and that the patient feeling well does NOT make it safe or deferrable; conveys this clearly as needing action TODAY

Arranges URGENT same-day HOSPITAL assessment (acute medical unit or emergency department, per local pathway), because UK Kidney Association guidance (2023) says potassium 6.5 mmol/L or more found in the community needs urgent hospital assessment for an ECG (hyperkalaemic changes — peaked T waves, widened QRS, etc.), repeat potassium/renal function and treatment — rather than a practice ECG first; the grade (mild 5.5–5.9, moderate 6.0–6.4, severe ≥6.5) sets the route, whatever the symptoms

Identifies and addresses the DRUG/INTAKE drivers: recently increased ramipril and spironolactone (advise to hold/stop per plan), and — by actively asking — the OTC IBUPROFEN (stop) and the POTASSIUM-BASED salt-substitute (stop), recognising these are key reversible contributors often missed
Takes a proper medication and intake history that captures OTC/non-prescribed items and salt substitutes (because the patient won’t volunteer them), and gives dietary high-potassium advice

Plans appropriate follow-up of renal function and a medication review (ACE inhibitor/spironolactone titration and monitoring — NICE NG106: check potassium and renal function after starting or changing these; NICE NG203: stop an ACE inhibitor/ARB if potassium rises to 6.0 or more once other potassium-raising drugs are stopped), and considers the precipitant for the creatinine rise (NSAID, dehydration, progression; possible AKI — NICE NG148)
Overcomes the deferral/dismissiveness without inducing panic: names the seriousness plainly, hears the stoicism and the hospital fear (the brother), and brings him to accept same-day care
Asks about OTC medicines and salt-substitutes in a way that makes disclosure easy and non-judgemental, rather than assuming the record is complete

Safety-nets clearly and acts: same-day hospital assessment route (ECG, repeat potassium, treatment), what to do if palpitations/chest pain/weakness/collapse occur (999), explicit stop/hold instructions for the culprits, confirms he will attend, and documents the plan and the recall

worked.txt: "I’m glad I caught you, and I’m sorry to ring you at work — but I did because it can’t wait. One of your blood results, your potassium, has come back high enough to matter today, even though you feel completely fine. Potassium is what keeps the heart’s rhythm steady, and at this level it can occasionally upset the rhythm, so I need to act now rather than at your next appointment."

"I know feeling well makes this hard to believe — and that’s exactly the catch with potassium: it often gives no warning until it causes a problem. So I’m not going to be reassured by you feeling grand; I’m going to be guided by the number, and the number says today."

"Let me ask a couple of things that really matter. We recently put your ramipril dose up, and you’re on spironolactone — both can raise potassium. But also: are you taking anything for that knee? … Ibuprofen, from the chemist. Right — that pushes potassium up too and isn’t on our records. And have you started any ‘low-salt’ or ‘heart-salt’ substitute? … You have? Those are usually packed with potassium. Together, that explains a lot — and it’s fixable."

"So, from now: stop the ibuprofen completely, and stop that salt substitute — go back to ordinary cooking without added salt. Hold your ramipril and spironolactone until you’ve been checked — don’t take today’s doses. We’ll sort your knee a safer way and review those heart/kidney tablets properly."

"Here’s what needs to happen now: at this level, you need to be seen at the hospital today — the assessment unit — for a heart tracing, an ECG, and your bloods repeated straight away, and treatment there to bring the potassium down safely if it’s still high. That’s what the kidney specialists’ guidance says for a potassium this high, rather than coming to us first. The delivery will have to wait. I’ll ring ahead and arrange where you go."

"I sense going in worries you — is that about hospitals? … Your brother. I’m sorry, and I understand. This is different: we’re acting early, on a number, to keep you safe, and most people are sorted the same day. If before you’re seen you get palpitations, chest pain, feel weak or faint — that’s 999 straightaway. I’ll confirm exactly where to go and follow up your repeat result. You feel fine, and I want to keep it that way — that’s why we move today."

f.learning: A potassium of 6.6 mmol/L is severe hyperkalaemia and a risk of life-threatening arrhythmia — and the patient feeling completely well does NOT make it safe or deferrable; hyperkalaemia is frequently silent until it causes a fatal rhythm. The action is urgent same-day hospital assessment (UK Kidney Association 2023: potassium 6.5 mmol/L or more in the community): an ECG (peaked T waves, widened QRS, etc.), an urgent repeat potassium/renal function and emergency treatment as needed — not a practice ECG first. The examinable clinical skill is finding the stacked, partly-hidden drivers: a recently increased ACE inhibitor and spironolactone (hold per plan), plus the contributors the record misses and the patient won’t volunteer — OTC NSAIDs (ibuprofen for his knee) and a potassium-based "low-salt" substitute (both stopped). The hidden agenda is deferral driven by stoicism and hospital fear (a brother who "never came home"), and the belief that OTC items "don’t count" as medicines. Convey urgency without panic, take an active OTC/salt-substitute history, give explicit stop/hold instructions and dietary advice, arrange same-day ECG/assessment, and safety-net cardiac symptoms to 999. He "feels fine" — hyperkalaemia is often asymptomatic until a fatal arrhythmia; muscle weakness/palpitations may or may not be present. Reassuring symptoms do NOT make a potassium of 6.6 safe. The challenge is conveying urgency to a well-feeling man who wants to defer.

knowledge.guideline: UK Kidney Association: Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults (updated 2023) · NICE NG203 (2021) · NICE NG106 (2018) · NICE NG148 (2019) · MHRA Drug Safety Update February 2016
knowledge.summary: A potassium of 6.5 mmol/L or more is severe hyperkalaemia: arrange urgent same-day hospital assessment, whatever the symptoms. Find and stop every driver, including the ones not on the record.

points.t: UK Kidney Association bands: mild 5.5–5.9, moderate 6.0–6.4, severe 6.5 mmol/L or more. Severe hyperkalaemia found in the community needs urgent hospital assessment for an ECG, repeat potassium and treatment. Moderate hyperkalaemia (6.0–6.4) needs an ECG; same-day hospital assessment if acutely unwell or with AKI; if well, repeat within 1 day after discussing with the renal/medical team.

Hyperkalaemia is often silent until it causes a rhythm disturbance. Weakness, palpitations or collapse may never come first. Act on the number, not on how well he feels. A haemolysed sample is possible, but never assume it when the drug history fits.

ACE inhibitor after a dose increase, spironolactone, CKD and heart failure, plus the two he has not mentioned: over-the-counter ibuprofen and a potassium-based salt substitute. The MHRA (Drug Safety Update, February 2016) warned of potentially fatal hyperkalaemia with spironolactone plus an ACE inhibitor or ARB, especially with renal impairment.

Stop the NSAID and the salt substitute now. Hold ramipril and spironolactone until hospital review. NICE NG203: stop ACE inhibitor or ARB if potassium rises to 6.0 mmol/L or more and other drugs that raise potassium have been stopped. The rising creatinine needs assessment for AKI (NICE NG148), where NSAIDs are a common precipitant.

Medication review with the heart-failure plan (NICE NG106 advises checking potassium and renal function after starting or changing these drugs). Reintroduce with monitoring. Low-potassium dietary advice; paracetamol or a non-NSAID plan for the knee. Potassium binders are options if RAAS therapy must continue: sodium zirconium cyclosilicate from a confirmed potassium of 5.5 mmol/L or more (NICE TA1148, April 2026, which updated and replaced TA599), or patiromer from 6.0 mmol/L or more (NICE TA623, 2020); sodium zirconium cyclosilicate may be started in primary care (UKKA July 2026), and neither replaces emergency treatment.

Confirm identity before sharing the result. State the seriousness plainly, ask actively about over-the-counter medicines and salt substitutes, give explicit stop and hold instructions, arrange where he goes, and name the 999 symptoms.

dg.d: Confirmed identity and privacy; explained why he was being called before asking questions; let him voice that he feels fine.
Work pressure, how he would get to hospital, the brother’s death in hospital and his dislike of being a bother.
Same-day hospital assessment: ECG, repeat potassium, renal function for possible AKI.
Drug-induced hyperkalaemia with rising creatinine; considered AKI from the NSAID; aware of a haemolysed sample but did not rely on it.
Asked about palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness, faintness and weakness; recognised 6.6 mmol/L as severe.
Severe hyperkalaemia from ramipril, spironolactone, ibuprofen and a potassium salt substitute on a background of CKD and heart failure.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Urgent hospital referral, explicit stop (ibuprofen, substitute) and hold (ramipril, spironolactone, metformin) instructions, safe transport.
Plans medication review, safer knee analgesia, low-potassium diet advice and renal follow-up.
999 symptoms named; referral phoned through; call documented; attendance checked.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up the knee (ibuprofen), ‘being good’ about salt (substitute) and the pause at ‘today’ (hospital fear).
Idea (routine bloods, can wait); concern (hospitals, being a bother); expectation (defer and sign for the delivery).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — "I don't want to be a nuisance." Underneath (only if asked): fear of hospital since your brother died there — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, is that Mr Raymond Childs? It’s Dr Lee from the surgery. Before I go on, can you confirm your date of birth for me? And are you somewhere you can talk for a few minutes?
model.why: Confirms identity and privacy before discussing a result

model.text: (Gives date of birth.) Yes, it’s me. You’ve caught me at work — is everything alright? The nurse said the bloods were just routine. I’ve got a delivery to sign for.

Thank you. I’m sorry to ring you at work, and I’ll be honest with you: I’ve rung because one of your results needs acting on today. Can I explain what it is, ask you a few quick questions, and then we’ll agree what happens next?
model.why: Honest about the reason for the call and sets the agenda

model.text: Today? I feel absolutely fine. Go on then.

It’s your potassium. It’s a salt in the blood that keeps the heart beating in a steady rhythm. Yours has come back at 6.6, which is high enough that it can upset the heart’s rhythm, even in someone who feels perfectly well.
model.why: States the value and why it matters in plain language

model.text: But I feel grand. Bit of a knee, that’s all. Can’t it wait for my next appointment?

I understand why you’d think that. The catch with potassium is that it usually gives no warning before it causes trouble. So I can’t be guided by how you feel; I have to be guided by the number, and at this level the number says today.
model.why: Explains that absent symptoms do not make severe hyperkalaemia safe

model.text: Right now, any fluttering or racing heartbeat, chest pain, breathlessness, dizziness, or your legs feeling weak?
model.why: Screens for symptoms that would need a 999 response

model.text: No. Nothing like that.
Good. Now I’d like to work out why it’s gone up. We increased your ramipril recently, and spironolactone can raise potassium too. Have you been taking both as prescribed?
Every morning, like clockwork.
You mentioned your knee. Are you taking anything for it, even something from the chemist or the supermarket? People often don’t count those, but they really matter here.
model.why: Picks up the knee cue and makes over-the-counter disclosure easy

model.text: Just ibuprofen. From the chemist. A couple a day. That’s not a proper medicine though, is it?

It’s a very common thing to take, so thank you for telling me. With your kidneys and heart tablets, ibuprofen can strain the kidneys and push potassium up. That may explain part of this. And have you changed anything in your diet lately, like a low-salt or heart-salt substitute?
model.why: Links the NSAID to the result and asks about salt substitutes

model.text: Actually, yes. I switched to one of those low-salt ones. For my blood pressure. Thought I was being good.

You were trying to look after yourself, and that’s exactly right in principle. Many of those substitutes swap the sodium for potassium, so for you they add potassium on top of everything else. Put together, the tablets, the ibuprofen and the salt substitute explain this. That’s the good news: it’s fixable.
model.why: Identifies the stacked drivers without blame

model.text: I’m going to suggest you’re seen at the hospital today. Before I do, I noticed you went quiet when I said ‘today’. What goes through your mind when I say hospital?
model.why: Responds to a cue and explores the fear behind the deferral

model.text: (Pause.) My brother went into hospital and never came home. I don’t like them. And I don’t like being a bother.

I’m sorry about your brother. That makes your reluctance completely understandable. This is different: we’ve found it early, on a blood test, before anything has happened. You’re not a bother. Acting now is how we keep it that way.
model.why: Acknowledges the fear and reframes early action as protective

model.text: So what would they actually do?

They’ll do a heart tracing, called an ECG, to check the potassium isn’t affecting the rhythm, repeat the blood test, and give treatment to bring the potassium down safely if it’s still high. They’ll also check your kidneys. How long you’re there depends on those results.
model.why: Explains the same-day assessment: ECG, repeat potassium, treatment

model.text: Until you’re seen: no more ibuprofen, stop the salt substitute completely, and don’t take any more ramipril or spironolactone. The hospital team will tell you when and how to restart them. Could you tell me back what you’re stopping?
model.why: Explicit stop and hold instructions with a teach-back

model.text: No ibuprofen, no low-salt stuff, and hold the ramipril and the spiro. Leave the metformin?

Good question. Please don’t take any more metformin until the hospital has checked your kidneys either; they’ll tell you when to restart. I’ll ring the medical team now and send them your results, so they’re expecting you. Is there a way you can get there without driving yourself?
model.why: Arranges the referral and a safe route to hospital

model.text: I can get a taxi. The delivery will have to wait, I suppose.
Thank you. If your work needs a note for the time off, we can sort that. Afterwards I’ll go through all your tablets with you, find a safer plan for the knee, and we’ll recheck your bloods.
model.why: Practical support and a named follow-up plan

model.text: One more important thing. If before you get there you notice palpitations, chest pain, feel faint or weak, or collapse, don’t wait for the taxi: that’s 999 straight away. Tell them your potassium was 6.6.
model.why: Names the 999 symptoms in plain words

model.text: Right. That’s clearer. I thought you were just being fussy at first.

I’d much rather be fussy today than sorry. So, to check we’re agreed: you’re going to the hospital this afternoon, you’ve stopped the ibuprofen and salt substitute, and you’re holding the ramipril, spironolactone and metformin until they advise you. Anything you want to ask?
No. I’ll go. Thanks for ringing, doctor.
Thank you, Mr Childs. I’ll record this call and check you arrived later today. Look after yourself.
model.why: Documents and closes the loop on attendance

social.t: He is at work and wants to sign for a delivery. Address the practical barrier (time off, a fit note if needed, safe transport) so the plan can happen.
His brother died after a hospital admission. Naming that fear, and explaining why this admission is different, is often what turns refusal into agreement.

legal.t: If he declines hospital, he is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005). Make sure he understands the specific risk, record the discussion and the advice given, and keep the door open.
He can self-certify for up to seven days; a fit note is needed after that if he is off longer.

professional.t: Confirm identity and check he can speak privately before sharing a result, especially at work (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).
A critical result needs a same-day, documented plan: who was told, what was advised, where the patient went and who checks the outcome (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).

community.t: Encourage him to tell the pharmacist about his kidney and heart medicines before buying anything over the counter. Kidney Care UK has patient information on potassium in food and salt substitutes.

redFlags: Palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness, faintness, collapse or muscle weakness — 999 now
Potassium 6.5 mmol/L or more — urgent hospital assessment regardless of symptoms
Rising creatinine, vomiting, diarrhoea or poor intake — possible AKI
psychosocial: At work, wants to defer; stoical and dislikes being a bother
Brother died after a hospital admission — the fear behind the deferral
Believes chemist medicines and salt substitutes ‘don’t count’
ice: Idea: routine bloods, he feels fine, so it can wait
Concern: hospitals (his brother) and being a nuisance
Expectation: to put it off until his next appointment

playbook.diagnosis: Be clear and calm: “Your potassium is 6.6. At that level it can upset the heart’s rhythm without warning, so it needs checking and treating today — and I think I know why it’s gone up.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Potassium is like the timing signal for your heartbeat. A bit too much and the signal can go wrong without any warning. Several things have been adding potassium at once — your tablets, the ibuprofen and the salt substitute — like several taps running into one bath.”

management.reflectIce: “After what happened to your brother, I understand why hospital is the last place you want to go. We’ve caught this early, on a blood test, and going today is how we keep you well.”
management.psychosocial: Remove the practical barriers: the delivery can wait, a fit note if needed, a taxi rather than driving, and a phone call ahead so he is expected.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment: ECG, repeat potassium, renal function and treatment
Stop ibuprofen and the salt substitute; hold ramipril, spironolactone and metformin until advised
Medication review, safer knee analgesia and low-potassium diet advice afterwards
safetyNet: 999 for palpitations, chest pain, faintness, weakness or collapse
Referral phoned through, call documented, attendance checked the same day

pitfalls.intro: This telephone station is failed on safety: deferring a severe result because the patient feels well, or missing the drivers he doesn’t volunteer. The marks come from urgency without panic and a careful medicine history.

items.fail: Booking a repeat potassium in a few days because he has no symptoms, or blaming a haemolysed sample.
items.why: Severe hyperkalaemia needs same-day hospital assessment whatever the symptoms. Examiners read deferral as “unsafe management of an abnormal result”.
items.fix: “At 6.6 I can’t rely on how you feel. You need a heart tracing and treatment today.”

items.fail: Checking only the repeat prescription list.
items.why: The ibuprofen and the potassium salt substitute are not on the record and he won’t volunteer them. Missing them leaves two causes running.
items.fix: Ask specifically: “Anything for the knee, even from the chemist? Any low-salt substitute?”

items.fail: Arranging hospital review but giving no instructions about his tablets.
items.why: Taking tonight’s ramipril and spironolactone adds to the problem. Vague plans are marked down.
items.fix: Name each item to stop or hold, then ask him to repeat the list back.

items.fail: Answering “I don’t like hospitals” with more facts about potassium.
items.why: The deferral is driven by his brother’s death, not by lack of information. Ignoring it loses the patient and the Relating marks.
items.fix: “What goes through your mind when I say hospital?” Then explain why this is different.

items.fail: Frightening him with cardiac arrest, then ending the call without agreeing where he goes.
items.why: Alarm without a plan increases avoidance and is poor safety-netting.
items.fix: Calm, clear urgency; phone the referral through; agree transport; check he arrived.

items.fail: Discussing the result before confirming who is on the phone and whether he can talk.
items.why: A confidentiality lapse is an easy professionalism mark lost.
items.fix: Name, date of birth, and “are you somewhere you can talk?” before any detail.

timeMap.d: Confirm who you’re speaking to and that he can talk. Say plainly that the result can’t wait.
Potassium 6.6, what it does to the heart rhythm, why feeling fine doesn’t make it safe. Screen for symptoms that mean 999 now.
Ramipril increase, spironolactone, then ask actively: anything for the knee? any salt substitute? The two hidden causes come out here.
Explore the pause at ‘hospital’ (his brother). Same-day hospital assessment. Stop and hold instructions with teach-back. Safe transport.
999 symptoms. Summary. Document, phone the referral through, check he arrived.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “I feel fine” and books a routine repeat; or alarms him without a plan; never asks about over-the-counter drugs or salt substitutes; leaves ramipril and spironolactone running; no 999 advice; no check that he will attend.
wordPics.pass: Recognises severe hyperkalaemia and arranges same-day hospital assessment with ECG; identifies ramipril and spironolactone and asks about other medicines; gives stop and hold instructions and a basic 999 safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: finds both hidden drivers through open, non-judgemental questions; explores the hospital fear and his brother without losing urgency; uses teach-back for the stop list; arranges safe transport, phones the referral through and checks attendance.

avoid.dont: “It’s probably a haemolysed sample — pop in for a repeat next week.”
avoid.instead: “At 6.6 I can’t assume it’s a lab error. You need a heart tracing and a repeat today.”
avoid.why: Deferring a severe result on the hope of a spurious sample is the unsafe choice examiners look for.

avoid.instead: “Are you taking anything for that knee, even from the chemist? And any low-salt substitute?”
avoid.why: A closed question lets him answer ‘no’; the hidden drivers only come out when asked specifically.

avoid.dont: “Your potassium is dangerously high and you could have a cardiac arrest.”
avoid.instead: “At this level it can upset the heart’s rhythm, so we act today, before anything happens.”
avoid.why: Urgency without panic keeps a frightened man engaged rather than avoidant.

SCA_MODELS.text: No. Nothing like that.
Good. Now I’d like to work out why it’s gone up. We increased your ramipril recently, and spironolactone can raise potassium too. Have you been taking both as prescribed?
Every morning, like clockwork.
You mentioned your knee. Are you taking anything for it, even something from the chemist or the supermarket? People often don’t count those, but they really matter here.
SCA_MODELS.why: Picks up the knee cue and makes over-the-counter disclosure easy

SCA_MODELS.text: Just ibuprofen. From the chemist. A couple a day. That’s not a proper medicine though, is it?

It’s a very common thing to take, so thank you for telling me. With your kidneys and heart tablets, ibuprofen can strain the kidneys and push potassium up. That may explain part of this. And have you changed anything in your diet lately, like a low-salt or heart-salt substitute?
SCA_MODELS.why: Links the NSAID to the result and asks about salt substitutes

SCA_MODELS.text: Actually, yes. I switched to one of those low-salt ones. For my blood pressure. Thought I was being good.

You were trying to look after yourself, and that’s exactly right in principle. Many of those substitutes swap the sodium for potassium, so for you they add potassium on top of everything else. Put together, the tablets, the ibuprofen and the salt substitute explain this. That’s the good news: it’s fixable.
SCA_MODELS.why: Identifies the stacked drivers without blame

SCA_MODELS.text: I’m going to suggest you’re seen at the hospital today. Before I do, I noticed you went quiet when I said ‘today’. What goes through your mind when I say hospital?
SCA_MODELS.why: Responds to a cue and explores the fear behind the deferral

SCA_MODELS.text: (Pause.) My brother went into hospital and never came home. I don’t like them. And I don’t like being a bother.

I’m sorry about your brother. That makes your reluctance completely understandable. This is different: we’ve found it early, on a blood test, before anything has happened. You’re not a bother. Acting now is how we keep it that way.
SCA_MODELS.why: Acknowledges the fear and reframes early action as protective

SCA_MODELS.text: So what would they actually do?

They’ll do a heart tracing, called an ECG, to check the potassium isn’t affecting the rhythm, repeat the blood test, and give treatment to bring the potassium down safely if it’s still high. They’ll also check your kidneys. How long you’re there depends on those results.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains the same-day assessment: ECG, repeat potassium, treatment

SCA_MODELS.text: Until you’re seen: no more ibuprofen, stop the salt substitute completely, and don’t take any more ramipril or spironolactone. The hospital team will tell you when and how to restart them. Could you tell me back what you’re stopping?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explicit stop and hold instructions with a teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: No ibuprofen, no low-salt stuff, and hold the ramipril and the spiro. Leave the metformin?

Good question. Please don’t take any more metformin until the hospital has checked your kidneys either; they’ll tell you when to restart. I’ll ring the medical team now and send them your results, so they’re expecting you. Is there a way you can get there without driving yourself?
SCA_MODELS.why: Arranges the referral and a safe route to hospital

SCA_MODELS.text: I can get a taxi. The delivery will have to wait, I suppose.
Thank you. If your work needs a note for the time off, we can sort that. Afterwards I’ll go through all your tablets with you, find a safer plan for the knee, and we’ll recheck your bloods.
SCA_MODELS.why: Practical support and a named follow-up plan

SCA_MODELS.text: One more important thing. If before you get there you notice palpitations, chest pain, feel faint or weak, or collapse, don’t wait for the taxi: that’s 999 straight away. Tell them your potassium was 6.6.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the 999 symptoms in plain words

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. That’s clearer. I thought you were just being fussy at first.

I’d much rather be fussy today than sorry. So, to check we’re agreed: you’re going to the hospital this afternoon, you’ve stopped the ibuprofen and salt substitute, and you’re holding the ramipril, spironolactone and metformin until they advise you. Anything you want to ask?
No. I’ll go. Thanks for ringing, doctor.
Thank you, Mr Childs. I’ll record this call and check you arrived later today. Look after yourself.
SCA_MODELS.why: Documents and closes the loop on attendance

SCA_STEM.name: Raymond Childs
SCA_STEM.recent: Monitoring bloods after the recent ramipril dose increase: potassium 6.6 mmol/L (flagged critical by the laboratory), creatinine mildly raised from his previous result. No ECG since the result.
SCA_STEM.reason: GP-initiated telephone call to discuss an urgent blood result. He is at work.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: UK Kidney Association: Treatment of Acute Hyperkalaemia in Adults (updated 2023) · NICE NG203 (2021) · NICE NG106 (2018) · NICE NG148 (2019) · MHRA Drug Safety Update February 2016
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A potassium of 6.5 mmol/L or more is severe hyperkalaemia: arrange urgent same-day hospital assessment, whatever the symptoms. Find and stop every driver, including the ones not on the record.

points.t: UK Kidney Association bands: mild 5.5–5.9, moderate 6.0–6.4, severe 6.5 mmol/L or more. Severe hyperkalaemia found in the community needs urgent hospital assessment for an ECG, repeat potassium and treatment. Moderate hyperkalaemia (6.0–6.4) needs an ECG; same-day hospital assessment if acutely unwell or with AKI; if well, repeat within 1 day after discussing with the renal/medical team.

Hyperkalaemia is often silent until it causes a rhythm disturbance. Weakness, palpitations or collapse may never come first. Act on the number, not on how well he feels. A haemolysed sample is possible, but never assume it when the drug history fits.

ACE inhibitor after a dose increase, spironolactone, CKD and heart failure, plus the two he has not mentioned: over-the-counter ibuprofen and a potassium-based salt substitute. The MHRA (Drug Safety Update, February 2016) warned of potentially fatal hyperkalaemia with spironolactone plus an ACE inhibitor or ARB, especially with renal impairment.

Stop the NSAID and the salt substitute now. Hold ramipril and spironolactone until hospital review. NICE NG203: stop ACE inhibitor or ARB if potassium rises to 6.0 mmol/L or more and other drugs that raise potassium have been stopped. The rising creatinine needs assessment for AKI (NICE NG148), where NSAIDs are a common precipitant.

Medication review with the heart-failure plan (NICE NG106 advises checking potassium and renal function after starting or changing these drugs). Reintroduce with monitoring. Low-potassium dietary advice; paracetamol or a non-NSAID plan for the knee. Potassium binders are options if RAAS therapy must continue: sodium zirconium cyclosilicate from a confirmed potassium of 5.5 mmol/L or more (NICE TA1148, April 2026, which updated and replaced TA599), or patiromer from 6.0 mmol/L or more (NICE TA623, 2020); sodium zirconium cyclosilicate may be started in primary care (UKKA July 2026), and neither replaces emergency treatment.

Confirm identity before sharing the result. State the seriousness plainly, ask actively about over-the-counter medicines and salt substitutes, give explicit stop and hold instructions, arrange where he goes, and name the 999 symptoms.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Confirmed identity and privacy; explained why he was being called before asking questions; let him voice that he feels fine.
Work pressure, how he would get to hospital, the brother’s death in hospital and his dislike of being a bother.
Picked up the knee (ibuprofen), ‘being good’ about salt (substitute) and the pause at ‘today’ (hospital fear).
Idea (routine bloods, can wait); concern (hospitals, being a bother); expectation (defer and sign for the delivery).
Same-day hospital assessment: ECG, repeat potassium, renal function for possible AKI.
Drug-induced hyperkalaemia with rising creatinine; considered AKI from the NSAID; aware of a haemolysed sample but did not rely on it.
Asked about palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness, faintness and weakness; recognised 6.6 mmol/L as severe.
Severe hyperkalaemia from ramipril, spironolactone, ibuprofen and a potassium salt substitute on a background of CKD and heart failure.
Urgent hospital referral, explicit stop (ibuprofen, substitute) and hold (ramipril, spironolactone, metformin) instructions, safe transport.
Plans medication review, safer knee analgesia, low-potassium diet advice and renal follow-up.
999 symptoms named; referral phoned through; call documented; attendance checked.

social.t: He is at work and wants to sign for a delivery. Address the practical barrier (time off, a fit note if needed, safe transport) so the plan can happen.
His brother died after a hospital admission. Naming that fear, and explaining why this admission is different, is often what turns refusal into agreement.

legal.t: If he declines hospital, he is presumed to have capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005). Make sure he understands the specific risk, record the discussion and the advice given, and keep the door open.
He can self-certify for up to seven days; a fit note is needed after that if he is off longer.

professional.t: Confirm identity and check he can speak privately before sharing a result, especially at work (GMC Confidentiality, 2017).
A critical result needs a same-day, documented plan: who was told, what was advised, where the patient went and who checks the outcome (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).

community.t: Encourage him to tell the pharmacist about his kidney and heart medicines before buying anything over the counter. Kidney Care UK has patient information on potassium in food and salt substitutes.

redFlags: Palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness, faintness, collapse or muscle weakness — 999 now
Potassium 6.5 mmol/L or more — urgent hospital assessment regardless of symptoms
Rising creatinine, vomiting, diarrhoea or poor intake — possible AKI
psychosocial: At work, wants to defer; stoical and dislikes being a bother
Brother died after a hospital admission — the fear behind the deferral
Believes chemist medicines and salt substitutes ‘don’t count’
ice: Idea: routine bloods, he feels fine, so it can wait
Concern: hospitals (his brother) and being a nuisance
Expectation: to put it off until his next appointment

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be clear and calm: “Your potassium is 6.6. At that level it can upset the heart’s rhythm without warning, so it needs checking and treating today — and I think I know why it’s gone up.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Potassium is like the timing signal for your heartbeat. A bit too much and the signal can go wrong without any warning. Several things have been adding potassium at once — your tablets, the ibuprofen and the salt substitute — like several taps running into one bath.”

management.reflectIce: “After what happened to your brother, I understand why hospital is the last place you want to go. We’ve caught this early, on a blood test, and going today is how we keep you well.”
management.psychosocial: Remove the practical barriers: the delivery can wait, a fit note if needed, a taxi rather than driving, and a phone call ahead so he is expected.
sharedPlan: Same-day hospital assessment: ECG, repeat potassium, renal function and treatment
Stop ibuprofen and the salt substitute; hold ramipril, spironolactone and metformin until advised
Medication review, safer knee analgesia and low-potassium diet advice afterwards
safetyNet: 999 for palpitations, chest pain, faintness, weakness or collapse
Referral phoned through, call documented, attendance checked the same day

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This telephone station is failed on safety: deferring a severe result because the patient feels well, or missing the drivers he doesn’t volunteer. The marks come from urgency without panic and a careful medicine history.

items.fail: Booking a repeat potassium in a few days because he has no symptoms, or blaming a haemolysed sample.
items.why: Severe hyperkalaemia needs same-day hospital assessment whatever the symptoms. Examiners read deferral as “unsafe management of an abnormal result”.
items.fix: “At 6.6 I can’t rely on how you feel. You need a heart tracing and treatment today.”

items.fail: Checking only the repeat prescription list.
items.why: The ibuprofen and the potassium salt substitute are not on the record and he won’t volunteer them. Missing them leaves two causes running.
items.fix: Ask specifically: “Anything for the knee, even from the chemist? Any low-salt substitute?”

items.fail: Arranging hospital review but giving no instructions about his tablets.
items.why: Taking tonight’s ramipril and spironolactone adds to the problem. Vague plans are marked down.
items.fix: Name each item to stop or hold, then ask him to repeat the list back.

items.fail: Answering “I don’t like hospitals” with more facts about potassium.
items.why: The deferral is driven by his brother’s death, not by lack of information. Ignoring it loses the patient and the Relating marks.
items.fix: “What goes through your mind when I say hospital?” Then explain why this is different.

items.fail: Frightening him with cardiac arrest, then ending the call without agreeing where he goes.
items.why: Alarm without a plan increases avoidance and is poor safety-netting.
items.fix: Calm, clear urgency; phone the referral through; agree transport; check he arrived.

items.fail: Discussing the result before confirming who is on the phone and whether he can talk.
items.why: A confidentiality lapse is an easy professionalism mark lost.
items.fix: Name, date of birth, and “are you somewhere you can talk?” before any detail.
